t: Number of Boomerangs — Counting Equal-Distance Pairs from Each Apex
o: We must count ordered triples (i, j, k) of distinct points where dist(i,j) = dist(i,k). The apex i is fixed first; j and k can be swapped, so each unordered pair {j,k} at equal distance contributes 2 boomerangs. In Example 1, point [1,0] is equidistant (distance 1) from both [0,0] and [2,0], giving the two ordered tuples. With n ≤ 500, an O(n²) or even O(n³) approach fits easily, but grouping by distance per apex gives a clean O(n²) solution.
k: For each apex i, only the multiset of squared distances to all other points matters.
If m other points share one distance from apex i, they contribute m*(m-1) ordered pairs (j,k).
Use squared distances to avoid floating-point sqrt errors entirely.

a.i: Directly enumerate every ordered triple (i, j, k) with distinct indices and check whether dist(i,j) equals dist(i,k). This mirrors the definition exactly and works because n ≤ 500 keeps n³ ≈ 1.25×10⁸ operations feasible in fast languages, though it's slow in Python.
s: Loop over apex i from 0 to n-1.
Loop over j ≠ i and k ≠ i, j ≠ k.
Compare squared distances dist2(i,j) == dist2(i,k); if equal, increment the answer.
a.t: O(n³) — three nested loops over all points; acceptable for n ≤ 500 but wasteful.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Map of Distances per Apex (Optimal)
a.i: Fix apex i and count how many points lie at each distance from it using a hash map keyed by squared distance. If m points share a distance, any ordered choice of two distinct ones forms a boomerang: m × (m−1) ways. Summing this over all distances and all apices gives the answer in O(n²), since each pair of points is examined once per apex.
s: For each apex i, create an empty hash map from squared distance to count.
For every other point j, compute the squared distance and increment its map entry.
After filling the map, add cnt * (cnt - 1) for every count cnt to the answer.
Clear/reuse the map for the next apex and return the total.
a.t: O(n²) — for each of n apices we scan all n points once; hash operations are O(1) average.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map holds at most n−1 distinct distances at a time.

w: In an interview, present the brute force briefly to show understanding, then pivot to the hash-map-per-apex approach as the intended O(n²) solution. Key pitfalls: forgetting that tuples are ordered (hence m*(m-1), not C(m,2)), using sqrt and floats instead of squared integers (precision bugs), and integer overflow when squaring coordinates up to 10⁴ (use 64-bit in Java/C++; Python and JS numbers are safe here since max squared distance ≈ 8×10⁸ fits in double/long). Edge cases: n = 1 or n = 2 always return 0. Follow-ups: counting unordered triples (divide by 2), handling duplicate points (problem guarantees uniqueness), or streaming/large-n variants where you'd need spatial partitioning like a grid or k-d tree.
